extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, and practitioners prosecuting chemical/biotech/pharmaceutical patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and examining Markush-type patent claims in chemical/biotech/pharmaceutical applications, focusing on clarity under 35 U.S.C. §112 and the propriety of Markush groupings. Covers statutory/ MPEP/ case-law tests, common pitfalls, examiner practice, and response strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirement under 35 U.S.C. §112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim clarity is required by 35 U.S.C. §112(b); current PTO policy emphasizes claim clarity (e.g., USPTO glossary pilot program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be sufficiently definite so that their metes and bounds are clear to a person of ordinary skill in the art; the PTO has initiatives to promote clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Markush claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush-type claim recites alternatives in a format such as 'selected from the group consisting of A, B and C.' The term 'Markush claim' here means any claim that recites a list of alternatively useable species regardless of format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the 'selected from the group consisting of' phrasing is common, the guidelines apply to any enumeration of alternatively usable species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consisting of vs. comprising (Markush phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to use the term 'comprising' instead of 'consisting of' in a Markush-type enumeration (Ex parte Dotter, 12 USPQ 382 (Bd. App. 1931)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct transitional/limiting language in Markush recitations to avoid form objections; follow MPEP guidance on proper phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double inclusion is not per se improper
rubrics_metrics.description: Double inclusion of an element by members of a Markush group (e.g., listing 'halogen' and separately 'chloro') is not, in itself, sufficient basis for objection or rejection (MPEP §2173.05(h)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject solely because of overlapping/generic vs. specific members; analyze context and whether grouping otherwise satisfies requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness test for Markush groups (breadth vs indefiniteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Breadth alone is not indefiniteness, but if a Markush group is so expansive that persons skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds (i.e., cannot envision all members), the claim may be indefinite under 35 U.S.C. §112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the test whether one of ordinary skill can envision all members; very large or amorphous lists can trigger indefiniteness rejections (citing In re Gardner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenus/genus claims are acceptable if supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus, subgenus, and Markush-type claims, if properly supported by the disclosure, are acceptable ways to claim inventions; examiners should not reject Markush-type claims merely because genus claims encompass them (MPEP §2173.05(h)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure adequate written description/support for genus/subgenus/Markush groupings in the specification to withstand challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process/combination vs. compound Markush grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Markush group occurs in a claim reciting a process or a combination (not a single compound), it is sufficient if the members of the group are disclosed to possess at least one property in common which is mainly responsible for their function in the claimed relationship; for single-compound claims members ordinarily must belong to a recognized physical/chemical or art-recognized class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different standards apply depending on whether claim is to a compound or to a process/combination — focus on the property responsible for function in process claims; disclose such common properties in the specification when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portions of chemical compounds: grouping determined by whole compound
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Markush expression is applied only to a portion of a chemical compound, the propriety of the grouping is determined by consideration of the compound as a whole, and does not depend on there being a community of properties in the members of the Markush expression (MPEP §2173.05(h)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the compound holistically when Markush terms target only a portion; do not require that listed substituents themselves share properties apart from the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are Markush claims 'generic' (propriety/test stringency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present practice holds that claims reciting Markush groups are not generic claims (MPEP §803); this may subject enumerated groups to a more stringent test for propriety of the recited members because enumeration is often used when no appropriate generic language exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that enumeration invites scrutiny of the propriety of included members; prefer genuine generic language only when appropriate and supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush Grouping doctrine (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim may be rejected under the judicially approved 'improper Markush grouping' doctrine when the claim contains an improper grouping of alternatively useable species (cases: In re Weber, In re Harnisch, Ex parte Hozumi; discussed in 2011 Guidelines and MPEP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper grouping is a case-by-case inquiry informed by case law and USPTO guidance; consult cited cases and 2011 Supplemental §112 Guidelines when assessing or asserting such rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush Grouping prong 1: single structural similarity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim contains an improper Markush grouping if the species of the Markush group do not share a 'single structural similarity' — i.e., they do not belong to the same recognized physical or chemical class or the same art-recognized class (Supplementary §112 Guidelines; MPEP §803.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a 'substantial structural feature' common to members exists and is essential to the claimed use; absence supports an improper grouping rejection (see Harnisch/Hozumi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush Grouping prong 2: common use requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim contains an improper Markush grouping if the species do not share a common use — meaning they are not disclosed in the specification or known in the art to be functionally equivalent (Supplementary §112 Guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the specification or the prior art supports a shared functional use among listed species; lack of such support justifies a grouping rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP §803.02 two-prong test (substantial structural feature + common use)
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP §803.02 explains a Markush grouping is proper when the embodiments share both a common use and a substantial structural feature essential to that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply both prongs: (1) substantial structural feature, and (2) common use that flows from that feature. If claim reads on patentably distinct inventions, a provisional election may be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the claim as a whole to determine whether the alternative species share a common use and a substantial structural feature essential to that use; if species lack either, or the shared structural feature is not essential to the common use, an improper Markush grouping rejection is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form ¶ 8.40 for improper grouping rejections and provide specific reasons why members do not share the structural feature and common use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner response options and applicant rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate applicant responses to an improper grouping rejection include amending the claims to include only species that share a single structural similarity and common use, or presenting a sufficient showing that the species in fact share such structural similarity and common use. An election of species can be required to conduct examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should either narrow claims, provide evidence of shared structure/use, or elect species for examination; examiners may extend search to related species sharing structure/use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form ¶ 8.40 Improper Markush Grouping Rejection template and examiner notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph provides boilerplate rejection language explaining that the improper Markush grouping includes species that do not share both a substantial structural feature and a common use that flows from it, and directs applicant to amend or show sufficiency. Examiner notes instruct to identify claim numbers, explain why members fail the test, and note election timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issuing such a rejection, the examiner should fill in claim numbers and specific deficiencies; form may only be used after applicant has made an election if an election is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searchability / procedural alternatives (election of species)
rubrics_metrics.description: If members of a Markush group are few or closely related so that search/examination of the entire claim can be made without serious burden, the examiner must examine all members; otherwise an election of species and directed examination may be required. Consider focusing on searchability or procedural steps (election + further searching) as alternatives to substantive rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use election and further search to manage examiner workload while preserving applicant rights; consider whether the proper remedy is procedural (e.g., restriction) vs. merits-based rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection vs. objection distinction for Improper Markush Grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate whether Improper Markush Grouping is a rejection (on the merits, appealable to the Board) or an objection/formal matter (reviewable by petition): MPEP §706.01 distinguishes rejections (merits) from objections (form). Historical guidance (Harnisch, 2011 Guidelines, Form ¶8.40) treats it as a rejection; current MPEP is less explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand procedural consequences: a rejection permits Board appeal under 35 U.S.C. §134; an objection is typically a formal matter only reviewable by petition to the Director. Cite authority and current MPEP when selecting classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-law guidance and limits (Weber, Harnisch, Hozumi, deGrado)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key cases provide instructive holdings: Weber emphasizes applicants' right to claim inventions and warns against administrative overreach; Harnisch found Markush groupings proper where compounds formed a subgenus with substantial structural similarity and common utility; Hozumi reversed improper grouping where structural feature essential to utility was disclosed; deGrado illustrates appellate procedural interplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case law to inform whether a grouping is 'improper' — focus on unity of invention, structural similarity, and disclosed common utility; recognize precedential status and nuances of each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush Clarity Scorecard (practical checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical categorization of common clarity issues: Reasonably clear items — 'consisting of' vs 'comprising', double inclusion, indefiniteness, subgenus claims, process/combination vs compound claims, portions of chemical compounds. Needs more clarity — 'Are Markush claims generic?' and 'Improper Markush Grouping'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this quick checklist when evaluating Markush claims to triage clarity issues and identify which require deeper analysis or policy clarification.
